lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4, what is a pixel? (One small square of colour in a picture made on a grid.) Today: how new technology, from the camera to the computer, changed art.
A camera obscura is a dark room or box with a small hole. Light from outside passes through and makes an upside-down picture inside. Ibn al-Haytham (about 965-1040) explained how it works.
In about 1826 Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest photograph that still exists; it needed hours of light. In 1839 Louis Daguerre showed a faster way, and photography spread round the world.
Painters no longer had to copy exactly: a camera could. Many tried new things instead. In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge's photos showed a galloping horse with all four hooves off the ground.
Film, from 1895, made pictures move. Digital art stores pictures as numbers: raster images as pixels, and vector images as points joined by curves.
Worked example: zoom into a raster circle and it turns into blocky squares. A vector circle is drawn again at every size from its points, so it stays smooth: good for logos.
Digital tools add layers, undo and copying. AI tools now make pictures from patterns learned from millions of images. That raises questions: who made it, and whose work did it learn from?
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, make a pinhole viewer from a box, foil and paper, and see the upside-down picture. Next: art about identity.

exercises.hint: Follow the light from the tree, through the hole, to the back of the box.
exercises.explain: The tree is the object; light goes through the pinhole into the dark box and makes the upside-down image at the back.

exercises.prompt: Why is the picture in a camera obscura upside down?
choices: light rays cross at the pinhole
exercises.hint: Follow a ray from the top of the tree through the hole.
exercises.explain: Light from the top of the tree goes down through the hole and lands low; light from the bottom lands high.

exercises.prompt: The first photographs needed only a split second of light.
exercises.explain: False: the first photograph needed hours of light; faster ways came later.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of image turns blocky when you zoom in?
exercises.hint: Think of what the picture is stored as.
exercises.explain: A raster image is a grid of pixels, so zooming in shows the squares.

exercises.prompt: A picture is 40 pixels wide and 30 high. How many pixels is it?
exercises.hint: Multiply the width by the height.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: a dark box with a hole
exercises.hint: Think of how each one makes or stores a picture.
exercises.explain: A camera obscura is a dark box with a hole; a photograph fixes light; raster is pixels; vector is points and curves.

exercises.prompt: Muybridge's photos showed that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves off the ground.
exercises.hint: What did the photos of 1878 freeze?
exercises.explain: True: his fast photos froze the moment no hoof touched the ground.

items: a logo that must work at any size
exercises.hint: Is it a grid of coloured squares, or shapes worked out from points?
exercises.explain: Photos, pixel art and scans are grids of pixels; logos and fonts are vectors so they stay sharp at any size.

exercises.prompt: A photo is 4,000 pixels wide and 3,000 high. How many million pixels (megapixels) is it?

choices: cameras could copy, so painters tried new things
exercises.hint: Think about what painters no longer had to do.
exercises.explain: A camera could record exactly, so many painters chose light, feeling and new ideas instead.

exercises.prompt: A raster picture 600 pixels wide is printed at 100 pixels a centimetre. How wide is the print in cm?
exercises.hint: How many hundreds of pixels are there?

exercises.prompt: An AI tool makes a picture in a living artist's style. What is a fair question to ask?
choices: whose work did it learn from?
exercises.hint: Think of where the AI's patterns came from.
exercises.explain: AI learns from millions of images, often people's art, so who made those and whether they agreed matters.

exercises.prompt: A vector logo stays smooth when it is made as big as a building.
exercises.hint: How is a vector image drawn again at a new size?
exercises.explain: True: it is worked out again from its points and curves at every size, so it never turns blocky.

exercises.hint: Use the timeline, and what you know of computers.
exercises.explain: The daguerreotype (1839), Muybridge (1878) and the first film show (1895) came before 1900; digital cameras (1975) and AI tools came after 1950.

exercises.prompt: Niépce's photograph needed hours of light. What did that mean?
choices: nothing moving could be caught sharply
exercises.hint: What happens to a moving thing during hours?
exercises.explain: In hours of light anything that moved was blurred or vanished, so early photographs showed still scenes.
